document.title: Fair-Weather No More: Guaranteed Efficiency in Secure Group Messaging

candidate.title: Computation-Sublinear Forward-Secure CGKA
candidate.subtitle: sublinear-time key refresh for updatable distributed broadcast encryption
candidate.category: Secure Group Messaging & Continuous Group Key Agreement
candidate.one_line: Is there a forward-secure continuous group key agreement scheme in which every operation, including the key-rotation refresh, runs in time sublinear in the group size -- not merely with sublinear communication -- where the paper commits to no specific rate (e.g. polylogarithmic) beyond sublinear?
candidate.informal: Continuous group key agreement (CGKA) protocols let a dynamic group of users maintain a shared secret, and achieving forward secrecy requires an explicit key-rotation ('refresh') step so that a later compromise of a user's state cannot expose past group keys. This paper builds the first CGKA scheme with forward secrecy whose communication cost is worst-case sublinear (in fact essentially independent) in the group size, by building a new primitive called updatable distributed broadcast encryption. But the scheme's refresh algorithms still take time that scales polynomially with the number of users in the group, because they take the group's membership as an explicit input and are allowed to touch all of it, even though the message they broadcast stays short. The paper explicitly poses the question of whether this can be avoided: is there a scheme with the same security guarantees whose refresh operation, like the group's other operations, runs in time sublinear in the group size -- the paper does not commit to a specific rate such as polylogarithmic for this question, only to sublinear? A strictly stronger version of the question, raised separately in a footnote, asks for refresh algorithms that do not take the membership set as an input at all and so run in time depending only on the security parameter; the paper shows a natural way of achieving that stronger property is completely insecure, by an attack that cancels out the encryption randomness between two users' ciphertext components, but this attack targets only that stronger variant and does not bear directly on the plain sublinear-refresh question stated above.
candidate.setting_latex:
An \emph{updatable distributed broadcast encryption} (updatable DBE) scheme is the cryptographic core of the paper's forward-secure CGKA construction. Users are identified by indices; each user $i$ holds a key pair $(\mathsf{pk}_i,\mathsf{sk}_i)$, and a set $S$ of currently active users has an aggregated public key $\mathsf{apk}$ together with, for each $i\in S$, an aggregated secret key $\mathsf{ask}_i$. A sender encrypts a single message to $\mathsf{apk}$, and every $i\in S$ decrypts it with $\mathsf{ask}_i$. Two update mechanisms are required: \emph{incremental} updates that add or remove one user from $S$, and a \emph{refresh} mechanism, run via algorithms $\mathsf{UpdPK}$ and $\mathsf{UpdSK}$, that re-randomizes every active user's keys at once. The refresh mechanism is what supplies forward secrecy: after a refresh, compromising a user's new secret key does not help decrypt ciphertexts sent before the refresh.

The paper's succinctness requirement asks only that the \emph{sizes} of $\mathsf{apk}$, of each $\mathsf{ask}_i$, and of the refresh ciphertext $\mathsf{ctref}$ produced by $\mathsf{UpdPK}$ be $\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)$, independent of $|S|$. It explicitly does \emph{not} require the \emph{running time} of $\mathsf{UpdPK}$ and $\mathsf{UpdSK}$ to be sublinear in $|S|$: both algorithms take the entire membership mapping $S$ as an explicit input and are allowed to touch every entry of it. The paper's own construction achieves compact keys and compact communication this way (built from a lattice-based matrix-commitment scheme under the decomposed learning-with-errors assumption~\cite{AMR25}, in the random oracle model), but its refresh algorithms run in time $\mathrm{poly}(\lambda,|S|)$. When this updatable DBE scheme is used to build a CGKA protocol, the resulting protocol inherits this asymmetry: its Add, Remove, and post-compromise-refresh operations all run in time independent of the group size, but its forward-secrecy refresh operation runs in time polynomial in the group size, even though the message it broadcasts remains short. The only prior CGKA scheme achieving forward secrecy at all, RTreeKEM~\cite{ACDT20}, does not meet even the paper's weaker (communication-only) efficiency requirements, so no scheme -- prior or from this paper -- achieves forward secrecy together with a sublinear-time refresh.
candidate.notation_latex:
$\lambda$: the security parameter.\\
$S$: a finite set of currently active group members, represented as a map from user indices to their public keys; $|S|$ is the group size.\\
$\mathsf{apk}$: the aggregated public key associated with $S$.\\
$\mathsf{ask}_i$: user $i$'s aggregated secret key.\\
$\mathsf{pk}_i,\mathsf{sk}_i$: user $i$'s individual public and secret key.\\
$\mathsf{ctref}$: the refresh ciphertext produced by $\mathsf{UpdPK}$ and consumed by $\mathsf{UpdSK}$.\\
$\mathsf{UpdPK}(\mathsf{pp},\mathsf{apk},S)\to(\mathsf{ctref},\mathsf{apk}',S')$: the public refresh algorithm, run by the sender of a refresh.\\
$\mathsf{UpdSK}(\mathsf{pp},\mathsf{ask}_i,\mathsf{ctref},S,\mathsf{pk}_i,\mathsf{sk}_i)\to(\mathsf{ask}_i',\mathsf{pk}_i',\mathsf{sk}_i',S')$: the private refresh algorithm, run by each recipient.\\
$\mathrm{poly}(\cdot)$: a fixed polynomial, used throughout to bound sizes and running times.
candidate.formal_statement_latex:
Fix the syntax and security notion for updatable distributed broadcast encryption exactly as in Definitions 5.6, 5.8 (or 5.9 for the adaptive case) -- static or adaptive semantic security under key-generation, corruption, add/remove, and refresh queries -- together with the succinctness requirement of Definition~5.6: the aggregated public key $\mathsf{apk}$, each aggregated secret key $\mathsf{ask}_i$, the refreshed public/secret keys, and the refresh ciphertext $\mathsf{ctref}$ output by $\mathsf{UpdPK}$ are all of size $\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)$, independent of the group size $|S|$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Open problem (Remark 5.7).} Does there exist such a scheme in which the refresh algorithms $\mathsf{UpdPK}(\mathsf{pp},\mathsf{apk},S)$ and $\mathsf{UpdSK}(\mathsf{pp},\mathsf{sk}_i,\mathsf{ask}_i,\mathsf{ctref},S)$ also run in time \emph{sublinear} in $|S|$, rather than merely producing succinct output while running in time $\mathrm{poly}(\lambda,|S|)$ as in this paper's Construction 5.10? (The paper does not commit to a specific target rate, such as polylogarithmic, for the refresh running time itself.)

Equivalently, phrased at the level of secure group messaging: does there exist a continuous group key agreement protocol that simultaneously achieves post-compromise security and forward secrecy while \emph{every} one of its operations -- including the forward-secrecy refresh operation, and not merely its communication -- runs in time sublinear in the current group size?

A strictly stronger variant, raised separately in Footnote~8 (page~7), asks for $\mathsf{UpdPK}$ and $\mathsf{UpdSK}$ to not take $S$ as an input at all, so that they run in time $\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)$ independent of $|S|$; the paper's Appendix~A gives an attack against a natural construction achieving \emph{that} stronger property (a common, rather than per-user, random shift), but this bears directly only on the stronger variant, not on the open problem above.

candidate.status_note: The paper's own construction (Construction 5.10) is succinct -- its aggregated keys and refresh ciphertext have size poly(λ), independent of |S| -- and is proved secure under the decomposed LWE assumption in the random oracle model, but its UpdPK/UpdSK refresh algorithms take |S| as an explicit input and run in time poly(λ,|S|). Remark 5.7 leaves open, without committing to a specific target rate, whether refresh can instead run in time sublinear in |S|; no construction achieving this, nor any proof that it is impossible, is known.
candidate.progress_note: As partial evidence of difficulty for a strictly stronger variant of this problem -- Footnote 8's request that UpdPK/UpdSK not take S as an input at all, running in time poly(λ) independent of |S| -- the paper's Appendix A analyzes a natural way to achieve that stronger property (giving every user the same shared random shift instead of a separate per-user shift derived from a random oracle) and shows it is completely broken by a 'zeroizing'/linear-cancellation attack: taking the public difference between two users' local openings and ciphertext components cancels the LWE randomization and exposes linear structure in the error term. This attack does not directly bear on the plain sublinear-refresh open problem (Remark 5.7), which permits UpdPK/UpdSK to still take S as input.

quotes.text: We leave it as an open problem to achieve a truly (computation-wise!) sublinear CGKA scheme with forward secrecy.

An important open problem is to obtain a scheme where the refresh operation requires sublinear running time. An updatable distributed broadcast encryption scheme with this property would yield a forward-secure CGKA protocol where computation and communication costs are all sublinear in the size of the group.

The refresh algorithms UpdPK and UpdSK take the mapping S as an explicit input, and as such, their running times are allowed to scale with the size of the group |S|. The only efficiency requirement we impose (see Definition 5.6) is that the size of the refresh ciphertext output by UpdPK be independent of the size of the group.

This seems challenging for the scheme we put forward in this paper, and indeed, in Appendix A, we describe a simple attack on a natural variant of our scheme that would satisfy this stronger efficiency requirement.

candidate.why_interesting: It pinpoints the exact remaining gap between 'communication-efficient' and 'fully efficient' forward-secure secure group messaging: the paper already achieves worst-case sublinear communication with forward secrecy from a falsifiable, plausibly post-quantum assumption, but computation is the one remaining barrier, and the paper backs the difficulty claim with a concrete attack against the obvious fix -- making this a well-posed target rather than a vague call for 'more efficient schemes'.
candidate.why_clean: The problem is stated purely in terms of the paper's own definitions (updatable DBE syntax, succinctness, and static/adaptive security), asks a sharp existence question with clearly delineated running-time bounds (poly(λ, log|S|) versus poly(λ, |S|)), and comes with a documented failed attempt -- the common-shift variant and its zeroizing attack in Appendix A -- that any attacker or prover can start from without needing unpublished machinery.
candidate.risks: A reviewer should keep the two grades of this question distinct: (i) Remark 5.7's plain request for sublinear (rate unspecified) refresh time while still taking S as input, which is what this statement asks, and (ii) Footnote 8's strictly stronger request to drop S as an input entirely and run in poly(λ), which is the variant Appendix A's zeroizing attack actually targets. A reviewer should also check whether some other lattice or algebraic technique (beyond the decomposed-LWE matrix-commitment approach used here) might achieve sublinear refresh time for (i) without needing a fundamentally new primitive, and since this is a very recent paper (2026), should search for contemporaneous follow-up work that may already bear on this question.

checks.name: existence
checks.finding: Found verbatim: 'We leave it as an open problem to achieve a truly (computation-wise!) sublinear CGKA scheme with forward secrecy.' (page 6). Restated formally in Remark 5.7: 'An important open problem is to obtain a scheme where the refresh operation requires sublinear running time.' (page 35). A second, stronger variant of the same question is raised in footnote 8 (page 7): removing S as an explicit input to UpdPK/UpdSK so the algorithms run in poly(lambda).

checks.name: openness
checks.finding: Read forward through the rest of the paper, including Appendix A (pages 71-74, the paper's final section). Appendix A gives a zeroizing attack on a natural sublinear-time variant of the refresh mechanism (Construction A.1, common shift Delta instead of per-user Delta_i); this is negative evidence, not a resolution. No later section, table, or footnote answers the question. The only other 'future work' items found in the paper (page ~62, active-adversary security) are unrelated to this problem. The open problem stays open through the paper's end.

checks.name: strength
checks.finding: The core question ('a forward-secure CGKA protocol where computation and communication costs are all sublinear in the size of the group', page 35) matches the draft's core claim at the right strength: same security notion (post-compromise security + forward secrecy, cf. footnote 4 page 4), same construction basis (Construction 5.10, decomposed LWE + random oracle). However, see check 4: the draft silently sharpens 'sublinear' into a specific asymptotic the paper does not commit to for this problem.

checks.name: quantifiers_and_parameters
checks.finding: The paper's own open-problem statement (Remark 5.7, page 35) asks only for 'sublinear running time' -- it never commits to poly(lambda, log|S|) for this specific question. The draft's formal_statement_latex asserts the target is exactly 'poly(lambda, log|S|)', which is the paper's general aspirational phrase used elsewhere for communication/aggregate-key size ('short (sublinear, and ideally, polylogarithmic...)', page 6-7) but not the phrase used for the refresh-time open problem itself. Separately, footnote 8 (page 7) poses an EVEN STRONGER, distinct variant: UpdPK/UpdSK dropping S as an input entirely, running in poly(lambda) with no dependence on |S| whatsoever (not even a log factor) -- and it is specifically THIS stronger variant, not the plain 'sublinear' open problem, that Appendix A's attack (Construction A.1, pages 72-74) targets. The draft's 'Equivalently' clause conflates these two distinct grades of the question into one statement, and its use of the Appendix A attack as 'partial evidence of difficulty' for the general sublinear-refresh question is really evidence about the harder, footnote-8 variant.

checks.name: attribution
checks.finding: This is the paper's own open problem about its own construction (Construction 5.10), not a problem it merely cites from elsewhere. RTreeKEM/ACDT20 is cited only as the prior (linear-communication) forward-secure CGKA scheme being improved upon (page 5), not as the source of this open problem.

checks.name: definitions
checks.finding: Definition 5.6 (Succinctness, page 35) requires apk, ask, the pk/sk output by UpdSK, and each pk_j in the refreshed mapping S' to be poly(lambda); Definitions 5.8/5.9 (pages 35-36) give exactly the static/adaptive security games with key-generation, corruption, and Add/Remove/Refresh update queries the draft describes. No notion has been silently swapped for a nonstandard one; the draft's summary omits mentioning individual pk/sk succinctness explicitly but does not contradict it.

checks.name: fabrication
checks.result: pass (one item flagged separately under quantifiers)
checks.finding: Bibliography keys checked against the paper's own reference list: ACDT20 appears at page 68 ('Joel Alwen, Sandro Coretti, Yevgeniy Dodis, and Yiannis Tselekounis...'); AMR25 appears at page 69 ('Damiano Abram, Giulio Malavolta, and Lawrence Roy...'). Both are genuinely printed-in-source-bibliography, not fabricated. The status_note's claims (Construction 5.10, decomposed LWE, random oracle model, refresh is the only linear-time operation) all check out against pages 5-7 and 35-39. The only unsupported-by-the-paper assertion found is the specific 'poly(lambda, log|S|)' target discussed under quantifiers.

checks.name: self_containment
checks.finding: formal_statement_latex uses UpdPK, UpdSK, apk, ask, S as if already defined, without inlining their syntax; the record provided to me has no separate notation_latex/definitions_latex fields to check them against, so I cannot confirm the full record is self-contained -- only that the definitions I could check (Definition 5.6, 5.8, 5.9) are represented faithfully where referenced.

corrections.problem: In formal_statement_latex, replace the specific target 'poly(lambda, log|S|)' for UpdPK/UpdSK running time with the paper's own (looser) phrasing: the open problem is whether refresh can run in time sublinear in |S| -- the paper (Remark 5.7, page 35, and page 6) never commits to a polylogarithmic bound for this question, only to 'sublinear'.

Separate the two grades of the open problem instead of merging them with 'Equivalently': (i) the base question (pages 6, 35) of making UpdPK/UpdSK run in sublinear (unspecified) time while still taking S as input, and (ii) the strictly stronger question raised only in footnote 8 (page 7) of removing S as an input entirely so the algorithms run in poly(lambda) independent of |S|. The zeroizing attack in Appendix A (pages 72-74) is evidence of difficulty specifically for (ii), not directly for (i); the status_note and formal statement should not present it as evidence against the general sublinear-refresh question without this distinction.

verify.reason: The open problem is genuinely posed by the authors (page 6, restated as Remark 5.7 on page 35) and genuinely stays open through the paper's end, including past the Appendix A attack (pages 71-74), which is a negative result on a natural variant rather than a resolution. However, the draft's formal statement sharpens the paper's own vaguer 'sublinear running time' target into a specific 'poly(lambda, log|S|)' bound the paper never states for this question, and it conflates that base open problem with a distinct, strictly stronger variant from footnote 8 (page 7) -- removing S as an explicit input entirely -- which is the variant the Appendix A attack actually targets.
